la:adv:heri.html:
hĕri or hĕre (in here neque e plane neque i auditur, :
here nunc e littera terminamus: at veterum comicorum adhuc libris invenio: Heri ad me venit, quod idem in epistulis Augusti, quas sua manu scripsit aut emendavit, deprehenditur,; cf. P.; ib.; v. esp. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 685), adv.
for hesi; cf. hes in hesternus; v. the letter R; kindred with Sanscr. hyas; Goth. gis-tra; Germ. gestern; Engl. yesterday; Gr. χθές, orig. χες
, yesterday.
Lit.
Form heri (perh. only so in Cic.): Septembris heri Calendae, hodie ater dies, Afran. ap. ; cf.: hoc heri effecit: hodie autem, etc., (al. here): ubi est hodie, quae Lyra fulsit heri?: heri jam edixeram omnibus,: quemne ego heri vidi ad vos afferri vesperi?: heri vesperi apud me Hirtius fuit,: heri vesperi,; : ut heri dicebam,; cf.: cum heri ipsi dixeris, te, etc.,: heri,; ; ; ; ; ; Afran. ap. et saep.—
Form here (a few times in Plaut., once in Cic., and after the Aug. per. most freq.): hoc here effecit,: res hodie minor est, here quam fuit, ac eadem cras, etc.,: here venisti mediā nocte,; ; : mihi quaerenti convivam dictus here illic De medio potare die,: hic here Phrixeae vellera pressit ovis,: dura, anime, dura, here fortior fuisti, Gallio ap. ; ; ; .—

la:noun:heres.html:
hēres (ēres, ), ēdis (archaic
acc. sing. herem, Naev. ap. ; ; cf. the art. † herem), comm.
Sanscr. har-āmi, seize; har-anam, hand; Gr. χείρ, χέρης; cf. erus
, an heir, heiress.
Lit.: testamento facto mulier moritur: facit heredem ex deunce et semuncia Caecinam, ex duabus sextulis M. Carm. 8, 6, 44: in testamento Ptolemaei patris heredes erant scripti ex duobus filiis major, et ex duabus ea, quae aetate antecedebat,: scripserunt heredes secum M. Crassum et Q. Hortensium,: aliquem heredem testamento relinquere,: relictus ab eo in amplis opibus heres,: aliquem heredem instituere,; ; cf.: per leges institui uxor non poterat heres,: instituto herede abdicato,: substitutus heres erat,: virgo Vestalis neque heres est cuiquam, etc., Labeo ap. : substituere heredem,: heres ex parte dimidia et tertia est Capito: in sextante sunt ii, quorum, etc.,: ex asse heres,sole heir,; so, heres ex parte sexta,: ex dodrante,: (L. Mescinius) heres est M. Mindio fratri suo,; so, cur virgini Vestali sit heres, non sit matri suae?; cf.: quem suis bonis heredem esse cupiebat,; and: atque meis bonis omnibus ego te herem faciam, Naev. ap. ; for which: quem quis heredem suum esse voluit,: repentinus heres,: liberti heredem sequantur,; so the formula frequently occurring on inscriptions: HIC LOCVS, HOC MONVMENTVM HEREDEM NON SEQVITVR, USU. abbreviated H. L. or H. M. H. N. S.,; ; ; 575; 2807; 4182; cf. opp.: HOC MONVMENTVM HEREDEM SEQVITVR,: heres secundus, the second heir, next heir, when the first dies: qui me secundum heredem instituerit. ; cf.: possessio heredum secundorum,: secundus,; ; ; also used of a female: Marcus ait: Heres ipsius secundus, de muliere loquens, P.: heres necessarius, a slave made heir with a grant of freedom, and compelled to assume the liabilities of the estate, Sandars: ideo sic appellatus, quia, sive velit sive nolit, omnimodo post mortem testatoris protinus liber et heres est,: heres suus et necessarius, a natural heir who was in the potestas of the deceased, , § 153; 156; ; opp.: heres extraneus,.— Poet.: tanti certaminis (i. e. armorum Achillis),.—

la:other:Hercules.html:
Hercŭles, is and i (the latter in Goer.; cf. Plin. ap. P.:
Herculei,), m., = Ἡρακλῆς, Etrusc. HERCLE (whence, by the insertion of a connecting vowel, the Latin form arose; cf. Alcumena for Ἀλκμήνη; v. also under B. the voc. hercle), son of Jupiter and Alcmena, husband of Dejanira, and, after his deification, of Hebe, the god of strength, and the guardian of riches, to whom, therefore, tithes were offered; he was also the guide of the Muses (Musagetes); the poplar was sacred to him, ; Varr. ap. ; Müll.; ; ; ; sq.; ; ; ; cf. with : neque Herculi quisquam decumam vovit umquam, si sapiens factus esset,: superavit aerumnis suis aerumnas Herculis,: Herculis Columnae, the Pillars of Hercules, i. e. the promontories between which is the Strait of Gibraltar, ; et saep.—In gen. plur.: et Herculum et Mercuriorum disciplinae, —Prov.: Herculi quaestum conterere, i. e. to squander everything (even the tithes of Hercules), : personam Herculis et cothurnos aptare infantibus,.—
Transf., analog. with the Greek Ἡράκλεις and Ἥρακλες, in voc.hercŭles, and more freq. hercŭle or hercle; also with a prefixed me: mĕ-hercŭles, mehercŭle (also separately: me hercule), and mĕhercle, as an oath or asseveration, by Hercules!
Hercules and mehercules: et, hercules, hae quidem exstant,; cf. Cael. ap. ; Poll. : licet, hercules, undique omnes in me terrores impendeant,; : neque, mehercules, hoc indigne fero,: cui, mehercules, hic multum tribuit,; Planc. ap. : at, mehercules, narrabit quod quis voluerit,.—
Hercule and mehercule, by Hercules! (in class. prose most freq.; cf. also: impetratum est a consuetudine, ut peccare suavitatis causa liceret: et pomeridianas quadrigas quam postmeridianas libentius dixerim, et mehercule quam mehercules,): et hercule ita fecit,: et hercule,; ; ; ; 12, 6, 4 al.: ac me quidem, ut hercule etiam te ipsum, Laeli, cognitio ipsa rerum delectat,: non hercule, Scipio, dubito quin, etc.,; ; : sed hercule facile patior datum tempus, in quo, etc.,, C, 10; ; : atqui nactus es, sed me hercule otiosiorem opera quam animo,: dicam me hercule,: non me hercule, inquit,: non mehercule,; : cognoscere me hercule, inquit, etc., Mai. N. cr.: ita mehercule attendi, nec satis intellexi, etc., Mos. N. cr.; : vere mehercule hoc dicam,: et mehercule ego antea mirari solebam, etc., ; : mihi mehercule magnae curae est aedilitas tua,: servi mehercule mei, si me isto pacto metuerent, etc.,.—
Hercle and mehercle (the former esp. freq. in Plaut. and Ter.; the latter very rare): malo hercle magno suo convivat, Enn. ap. (Sat. v. 1 Vahl.): obsecro hercle, quantus et quam validus est,; : tanto hercle melior,: mihi quidem hercle non fit verisimile,: nescio hercle,; : perii hercle,; ; : non hercle,: per hercle rem mirandam (i. e. permirandam) Aristoteles dicit,.—With intensive particles: heu hercle,: scite hercle sane,; cf.: sane quidem hercle,: minime, minime hercle vero!; cf.: minime hercle,: haudquaquam hercle, Crasse, mirandum est, etc.,: pulchre mehercle dictum et sapienter,; .
Derivv.
Hercŭlĕus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hercules, Herculean: domiti Herculea manu Telluris juvenes,: labor,: coronae arbos,i. e. the poplar,; cf.: umbra populi,: leo,the lion's skin worn by Hercules,: Oete,on which Hercules burned himself,: hospes,i. e. Croto, by whom Hercules was hospitably entertained,: ternox,in which Hercules was begotten,: hostis,i. e. Telephus, son of Hercules,: gens,i. e. the family of the Fabians sprung from Hercules,; so, penates,: sacrum,instituted by Evander in honor of Hercules,: Trachin,built by Hercules,: urbs,the city of Herculaneum, built by Hercules,.—Hence also: litora,near Herculaneum,: Tibur,i. e. where Hercules was worshipped,; : astrum,i. e. the constellation of the Lion,: fretum, i. e. the Pillars of Hercules, (Strait of Gibraltar), ; also: metae,.—
Hercŭlā-nĕus, a, um, adj., the same: pars, i. e. the tithes (dedicated to Hercules), the tenth part, .—Also to denote things large of their kind: formicae,. 4, 10, § 29: urtica,: nodus,: nymphaea,: sideritis,: machaera,.—
Hercŭlānus, a, um, adj., the same: pes, i. e. long, large (cf. in the preced.), .—
Acc. to the Gr. form Hēraclēus or Hēra-clĭus, a, um, adj., = Ἡράκλειος or Ἡράκλιος, the same: fabulae, (al. acc. to the MSS. Herculeias).—
Hēraclī-des, ae, m., = Ἡρακλείδης, a male descendant of Hercules, Heraclid: exclusi ab Heraclīdis Orestis liberi,—
Hercŭlĭus, i, m., a surname of the emperor Maximinianus, and hence, Her-cŭlĭāni, ōrum, m., his guards, ; .
